findings.title: [P1] Restrict login redirects to trusted same-origin paths
findings.body: When `returnUrl` comes from login request state, an attacker can supply an external destination and send an authenticated user to a phishing site immediately after login. Validate and allow only trusted same-origin paths before navigation.

findings.title: [P1] Do not write issued tokens to application logs
findings.body: Every issued token is forwarded unchanged to `console.log`. In deployments that retain or export console output, anyone with log access can recover active bearer credentials and impersonate users. Audit only non-sensitive metadata or a non-reversible identifier.

findings.title: [P1] Redact issued tokens before auditing
findings.body:
Every live token passed to `recordIssuedToken` is emitted verbatim through `console.log`, exposing bearer credentials to browser consoles or centralized server logs and anyone with access to them.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restrict login return URLs to trusted same-origin paths
findings.body:
Passing an attacker-controlled value such as `https://attacker.example` redirects an authenticated user off-site. Login flows commonly source return URLs from requests, enabling phishing and redirect-chain abuse unless the scheme and origin are validated.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restrict login redirects to trusted same-origin URLs
findings.body:
An attacker-controlled `returnUrl`, including `https://attacker.example` or a `javascript:` URL where browser policy permits it, is passed directly to a navigation sink. This enables post-login open redirects and potentially same-origin script execution instead of the previous fixed `/dashboard` destination.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Do not write issued tokens to application logs
findings.body:
Every call records the raw issued token through `console.log`. In environments where logs are retained, exported, or accessible to operators or logging vendors, anyone with log access can recover active credentials and impersonate users.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
